lessons.title: Slab Myths: Will a Raise Really Cut Your Take-Home Pay?

body.text: Almost every raise leaves you richer. The slab table alone can never make a raise cost you money. Only three narrow zones created by the rebate and surcharge can, and even there the loss is small and avoidable.

children.text: Office canteens, WhatsApp groups and Instagram finance reels are full of confident tax claims. Some are flatly wrong, some are half right, and a few are true only inside a band of income a few thousand rupees wide. You now have every tool needed to test them. This lesson takes the eight most common slab myths and gives each a verdict.

body.caption: Eight Slab Myths at a Glance

cells: "A raise into a higher slab will cut my take-home pay"
False, except in three narrow zones
"I'm in the 30% slab, so I pay 30% tax"
"Income up to ₹12 lakh is tax-free for everyone"
"If my CTC is above ₹12.75 lakh, I will definitely pay tax"
"Selling shares will push my salary into a higher slab"
False, but gains can still raise your tax on salary

children.text: Myth 1: "A Raise Into a Higher Slab Will Cut My Take-Home Pay"

Verdict: false on the slab table. Because each slab rate applies only to income inside that slab, crossing a threshold never raises tax on the income you already had. The highest possible marginal slab rate is 30%, so from the slabs alone you keep at least ₹68.80 of every extra ₹100, after cess and before surcharge. Take Arvind, whose Total Income rises from ₹16 lakh to ₹18 lakh, pushing him into the 20% slab. His tax rises by ₹41,600 and he keeps ₹1,58,400 of the ₹2,00,000 raise.
The myth survives because of three genuine exceptions, all created by adjustments that sit on top of the slabs rather than by the slabs themselves.

body.caption: The Only Three Zones Where Earning More Can Leave You With Less

cells: Rebate lost; marginal relief caps tax at the excess, but 4% cess is added on top
Rebate lost with no marginal relief
10% surcharge on all tax; marginal relief caps it, but cess is added on top

body.title: Income Left After Tax Around the ₹12 Lakh Rebate Edge (New Regime, Resident)

body.text: Look at the scale of the dip. Between ₹12 lakh and about ₹12.74 lakh, take-home falls by at most around ₹2,800, then climbs steadily. A raise from ₹12 lakh to ₹13 lakh still leaves you ₹22,000 better off. Turning down a raise over this is a mistake; restructuring it, for example through employer NPS, is the smart response.

body.title: Show me the math: the old regime cliff at ₹5 lakh

children.text: At exactly ₹5,00,000, an old regime taxpayer below 60 has ₹12,500 of slab tax, fully cancelled by the rebate. At ₹5,00,001 the rebate disappears and tax with cess is about ₹13,000, so one extra rupee costs about ₹13,000. Above ₹5 lakh, each extra rupee adds 20% tax plus cess, so income after tax is ₹5,00,000 + 0.792E − ₹13,000, where E is the income above ₹5 lakh. This climbs back to ₹5,00,000 only when E reaches about ₹16,414. At ₹5,10,000, tax is ₹15,080 and income after tax is ₹4,94,920, still ₹5,080 below where the taxpayer started.
Myth 2: "I'm in the 30% Slab, So I Pay 30% Tax"

Verdict: false. 30% is the marginal rate on income above ₹24 lakh under the new regime. The effective rate is far lower: 16% of Total Income at ₹30 lakh and 21.6% at ₹50 lakh, before cess. Chapter 2 covers the difference in full.
Myth 3: "Income Up to ₹12 Lakh Is Tax-Free for Everyone"

Verdict: partly true. It holds for a resident individual under the new regime whose income is taxed at slab rates. It fails for non-residents, HUFs and firms, who get no rebate. It fails for old regime taxpayers, whose rebate stops at ₹5 lakh. And it fails for anyone with special-rate income: a resident with ₹10 lakh of salary income and ₹1 lakh of short-term equity gains still pays ₹20,800 on the gains.
Myth 4: "If My CTC Is Above ₹12.75 Lakh, I Will Definitely Pay Tax"

Verdict: false. The ₹12.75 lakh figure applies to taxable gross salary, not CTC. Ravi, a resident at a Noida IT firm, has a CTC of ₹13,50,000 that includes ₹60,000 of employer PF and a ₹24,050 gratuity provision, neither taxable this year. His taxable gross salary is ₹12,65,950 and his Total Income after the standard deduction is ₹11,90,950. Slab tax of ₹59,095 is fully cancelled by the rebate. His CTC is ₹75,000 above the "limit" and he pays zero.

body.title: What People Say vs What the Law Says

columns.label: The Myth
points: 5. Senior citizens always get better slabs
6. Selling shares pushes my salary into a higher slab
8. The rebate is just another deduction

columns.label: The Reality
points: 5. Only under the old regime. The new regime has one table for every age, with a ₹4 lakh nil slab that beats even the ₹3 lakh senior limit
6. Special-rate gains never change your slab rates, but they count towards Total Income and can cost you the rebate or trigger surcharge
7. A deduction saves tax at your marginal rate, so ₹10,400 at the 20% slab. The exception: inside a relief zone, the saving can exceed 100%
8. A deduction reduces income; the rebate reduces tax itself, rupee for rupee, and vanishes above its income limit

body.title: Myth or Fact? Flip to Check

cards.term: "Moving from the 15% slab to the 20% slab raises tax on all my income."
cards.definition: Myth. Only income above ₹16 lakh is taxed at 20%. Tax on the first ₹16 lakh stays ₹1,20,000.

cards.term: "A resident with ₹12 lakh of salary income and no other income pays zero tax under the new regime."
cards.definition: Fact. Slab tax of ₹60,000 is fully cancelled by the rebate, so cess is zero too.

cards.term: "An NRI with ₹8 lakh of rent from India pays no tax because income is below ₹12 lakh."
cards.definition: Myth. Non-residents get no rebate. Slab tax of ₹20,000 plus ₹800 cess applies.

cards.term: "A 70-year-old pays the same new regime slab tax as a 30-year-old on the same income."
cards.definition: Fact. The new regime has no age-based slabs.

cards.term: "₹3 lakh of long-term equity gains will push my ₹20 lakh salary into the 25% slab."
cards.definition: Myth. Salary slab tax stays ₹2,00,000. The gains are taxed separately at 12.5% above ₹1,25,000.

cards.term: "Earning ₹12.3 lakh instead of ₹12 lakh can leave me with slightly less after tax."
cards.definition: Fact. Marginal relief caps tax at the ₹30,000 excess, but 4% cess makes it ₹31,200, so take-home drops by ₹1,200.

cards.term: "Surcharge applies only to the income above ₹50 lakh."
cards.definition: Myth. Once Total Income crosses ₹50 lakh, surcharge applies to the entire income tax, softened only by marginal relief near the threshold.

body.title: How Much of the Raise Is Kept?
body.prompt: Swati, a resident chartered accountant in Jaipur on the new regime, gets a raise that takes her Total Income from ₹20,00,000 to ₹23,00,000, all slab-rate income. How much of the ₹3,00,000 raise does she keep after tax, including cess?
body.explanation: The whole ₹3,00,000 falls in the 25% slab (₹20 to ₹24 lakh). Extra tax is 25% of ₹3,00,000 = ₹75,000, plus 4% cess of ₹3,000, a total of ₹78,000. She keeps ₹2,22,000, or 74% of the raise. Moving into the 25% slab did not touch the tax on her first ₹20 lakh.

body.title: Spot the True Statement
body.question: Which of these statements about the new regime is true?
options: A resident earning ₹13 lakh of Total Income takes home less than one earning ₹12 lakh
A resident earning ₹12,50,000 of Total Income takes home slightly less than one earning ₹12,00,000
Senior citizens get a ₹5 lakh nil slab
Long-term equity gains are added to salary and taxed at slab rates
body.explanation: At ₹12,50,000, marginal relief caps tax at ₹50,000, and cess makes it ₹52,000, leaving ₹11,98,000, which is ₹2,000 less than at ₹12 lakh. At ₹13 lakh, tax is ₹78,000 and take-home is ₹12,22,000, so option A is false. The ₹5 lakh nil slab is for super senior citizens under the old regime only, and long-term equity gains are taxed at a special rate.

body.title: Why Raises Rarely Hurt
body.textWithBlank: Crossing into a higher slab never raises tax on your existing income, because each slab rate applies only to the income ___ that slab.
body.explanation: Each slab is a separate bucket. Only the rupees that spill into a new bucket are taxed at its rate; the buckets below are unaffected.

body.title: Should Pradeep Refuse His Increment?
body.scenario: Pradeep, a resident accounts executive in Kanpur on the new regime, has Total Income of ₹12,00,000 and pays no tax. His annual increment will take Total Income to ₹12,40,000. His brother-in-law tells him: "Refuse it or ask them to hold it back. You'll pay tax and end up with less money." Pradeep's basic salary is ₹5,00,000 and his employer offers NPS contributions of up to 14% of basic.
body.prompt: Is the brother-in-law right? What should Pradeep do?
body.modelAnswer: He is right about the numbers but wrong about the solution. At ₹12,40,000, slab tax is ₹66,000, marginal relief caps it at the ₹40,000 excess, and cess makes it ₹41,600. Take-home would be ₹11,98,400, ₹1,600 less than today. But refusing the increment throws away ₹40,000 a year of pay, and next year's increment will likely push him out of the zone anyway. The better move is to ask HR to route ₹40,000 of the increment into employer NPS, well within his 14% limit of ₹70,000. His Total Income stays at ₹12,00,000, he pays zero tax, and he still gets all ₹40,000, just in his retirement account. Once his income grows past about ₹12.74 lakh, the zone stops mattering and every increment adds to his take-home.

points: Slab rates alone can never make a raise reduce your take-home pay
Only three narrow zones can: just above ₹12 lakh (new regime), just above ₹5 lakh (old regime) and just above ₹50 lakh (surcharge), with small losses
Your top slab rate is your marginal rate, not your effective rate
The ₹12 lakh zero-tax promise covers only resident individuals' slab-rate income under the new regime
The ₹12.75 lakh figure applies to taxable gross salary, not CTC
Special-rate income never changes slab rates but can cost you the rebate or trigger surcharge
If a raise lands you in a dip zone, restructure it, for example through employer NPS, instead of refusing it

body.text: Figures assume individuals with only slab-rate income for tax year 2026-27, unless stated. Zone boundaries are approximate and change if rates or limits change in a Budget. This lesson is for education only and is not tax advice.
